title: The Day You Are Born Sets Your Layer

scenes.tts: In the mouse cortex, the first cortical plate neurons end up deepest, beside the white matter. Neurons born days later end up near the surface. Yet these neurons are made near the ventricle, below. So the later neurons must climb past the cortical plate neurons made before them. How does a neuron's birthday decide where it settles?
scenes.visual: A slice of cortex with ventricle at the bottom and surface at the top. A first-born neuron rises to a deep spot; a later one rises past it, with a question mark.
scenes.narration: In the mouse cortex, the first cortical plate neurons end up deepest, beside the white matter. Neurons born days later end up near the surface. Yet these neurons are made near the ventricle, below. So the later neurons must climb past the cortical plate neurons made before them. How does a neuron's birthday decide where it settles?

scenes.tts: Progenitors line the ventricle. They divide, and the new neurons travel outward. The first to leave form a thin sheet under the outer surface, the preplate. The next wave settles inside the preplate and splits it in two. The outer part is the marginal zone. The inner part is the subplate. Each later wave passes the neurons already there and settles above them. Layer six is made first. Layer two is made last.
scenes.visual: Pink preplate band forms at the top, splits into marginal zone and subplate as the first cohort enters; three more cohorts pass and stack above, labelled layer 6 first, layer 2 last.

scenes.tts: How do you know when a neuron was born? You date its last S phase, when DNA is copied. Give a pregnant mouse one dose of thymidine carrying tritium, a radioactive form of hydrogen. Only cells copying DNA in the next hour or so are marked. A cell that divides again halves its label. So a neuron that stays heavily labeled made its last copy while the label was there. The label marks that moment. It tells the cell nothing.
scenes.visual: A pulse of labeled thymidine reaches two cells copying DNA. One leaves the cycle and stays heavily labeled; the other divides and its daughters carry half the label each.
scenes.narration: How do you know when a neuron was born? You date its last S phase, when DNA is copied. Give a pregnant mouse one dose of thymidine carrying tritium, a radioactive form of hydrogen. scenes.tts: In 1961, Jay Angevine and Richard Sidman gave pulses on different embryonic days. Cells labeled earliest lay deepest. Cells labeled on later days lay nearer the surface. This ruled out a simple idea. If new cells just shoved older ones outward, the earliest cells would end up on top. They ended up on the bottom. Later cells passed them.
scenes.visual: Pulses on early to late days light up cohorts from deep to surface; a mini column shows the shoving prediction with the earliest on top, crossed out.
scenes.narration: In 1961, Jay Angevine and Richard Sidman gave pulses on different embryonic days. Cells labeled earliest lay deepest. Cells labeled on later days lay nearer the surface. scenes.tts: Does the progenitor carry its own schedule, or do its surroundings tell its daughter where to go? Susan McConnell moved ferret progenitors that make deep-layer neurons into an older host. Cells moved while copying DNA mostly settled in the upper layers, like the host's own neurons. Cells moved later in the cycle mostly settled in the deep layers. Their fate was already fixed. Late progenitors put into a young host still made upper-layer neurons.
scenes.visual: A deep-layer progenitor is placed into an older host at S phase, and its daughter turns upper-layer colour; moved later, the daughter stays deep. Then a late progenitor in a young host still makes an upper-layer neuron.
scenes.narration: Does the progenitor carry its own schedule, or do its surroundings tell its daughter where to go? Susan McConnell moved ferret progenitors that make deep-layer neurons into an older host. Cells moved while copying DNA mostly settled in the upper layers, like the host's own neurons. Cells moved later in the cycle mostly settled in the deep layers. Their fate was already fixed. Late progenitors put into a young host still made upper-layer neurons.

scenes.tts: So a neuron's birthday predicts its layer. Early neurons sit deep. Later neurons pass them and settle above. In ferret experiments, a progenitor's choices narrow with time, and they do not reverse. This is a strong tendency of the mammalian neocortex, with some overlap between days. Keep the rule. When a neuron is born predicts where it settles.
scenes.visual: Full cortex slice with a time arrow along it; a menu of fates beside it shrinks from four to three to two as the progenitor ages.
